Notes on a Format

The Quiet Durability of Plain Text

A short demonstration article for the selection translation overlay. Select any sentence to see the cairn-red trigger; click it to open the streaming card.

Plain text is the most durable format we have. It has survived every operating system, every editor, and every decade of hardware churn, because it asks for nothing but a way to read bytes. When a document is written in plain text, the tooling around it can change without touching the words themselves.

Consider what happens when you open a file that was written thirty years ago. A word processor may refuse it, a proprietary format may have lost its decoder, but a plain text file still opens in a terminal, in an editor, in a browser, on a phone. The format does not depend on a vendor, a license, or a version number. That is not a technical achievement so much as a refusal to be clever: the file says what it means, and nothing else. This is why notes, logs, source code, configuration, and correspondence have all converged on it, and why the tools built around it can be replaced one by one without losing the record. The document is not the application. The document is the words.

Reading, too, benefits from this restraint. A page of plain text has no chrome to distract from the sentence, no layout to negotiate with, no hidden state. What remains is the thing itself: a line of thought, set down and left alone.
